name: Omar Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The bakery accounts are usually first because a missing invoice can hold up the whole return. I use an AI checker to find odd entries, then lay the invoice beside my screen so Saira can see why I changed one. I am 43 and have a bachelor’s degree in accounting, but I am still a junior here and learning the tricky tax rules; I like a good puzzle, though I can feel the school pickup deadline coming.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your household situation, and how are the finances?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Clara, my partner, cooks at a school, and our children Ana and Luis are both school age. We pay a mortgage; my accounting pay is typical, and we have around three months of expenses saved. There are some similar firms nearby, and I use AI tools every day, but Clara and I budget around two wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would still have tax season and the bakery owners calling about receipts. A faster search would give me a better Tuesday, not a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my coworkers that routine sorting is useful if we can show the source for every number. I use AI every day for first-pass checks, but I still send my work to the senior reviewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For my household this is fairly steady: my salary is normal for a junior accountant and we have three months of expenses saved. The mortgage still needs two wages, but some firms nearby could hire if I needed a change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep handling the same small business accounts and continue checking the AI flags against invoices each morning. I would also move a fixed amount from each monthly pay cheque into our emergency account until it covers four months, while my partner Clara keeps the usual grocery budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the job in this picture, although I never forget the mortgage date. The time-saving tool would make me less late for the school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does checking the flags involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI checker marked a bakery oven repair as a new asset, and I corrected it from the invoice before my supervisor saw the file. I like the speed, but that sort of mistake is why I keep the source open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you save each month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could move thirty from my pay without touching Clara’s income. It is not a fortune, but it is new cash added to the reserve.

say: I would say **routine sorting** helps only when every figure links to a source.
I would tell coworkers I still use a **senior reviewer** despite daily AI checks.
think: Our **three-month reserve** and normal pay keep the mortgage manageable.
I know the AI can **misclassify invoices**, even in a mild change.
do: Check daily **AI flags** against invoices on the same accounts.
Transfer **thirty monthly** from salary until emergency savings cover four months.
feel: I feel **calm** about work, while watching the mortgage date.
S0.quote: The AI checker marked a bakery oven repair as a new asset, and I corrected it from the invoice before my supervisor saw the file.
fieldNote: He uses AI **every day** but has caught a concrete oven-repair misclassification.
A new **thirty-monthly transfer** from pay grows the household reserve without assuming a windfall.

steps.text: Keep checking AI flags against invoices on current accounts
Transfer thirty monthly from salary until emergency savings cover four months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This reaches the draft and checking work I do most days. The tool could make me faster and make my place easier to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the office to test the software on old returns with known errors before counting saved hours. I would also say junior accountants need real review practice, not only a screen that shows green.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the firm could cut my junior hours even if I am good with AI, because I am still learning the tax rules. Clara works as a school cook, but her wage would not cover our mortgage and two children on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would take the firm’s paid error-review workshop if the seat is confirmed, then test its approved tool on old returns with client details removed. If my paid hours drop in the first year, I would apply only to posted junior accounts jobs with a stated wage that still covers our fixed bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because I can improve a task and still lose hours on it. Three months of savings gives me search time, not a second salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the workshop yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the firm has a training budget and I would use a paid seat if one is available. If no seat opens, I would keep my current work and use the free practice examples from my professional association at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show in an interview elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the correction log for returns I reviewed, with client details removed. I would not leave for a vacancy without written pay and a start date, because the mortgage runs every month.

say: I would ask for **known-error testing** before the firm counts saved hours.
I would say juniors still need **real review practice**.
think: My **junior hours** could fall despite daily AI use.
Clara’s school-cook wage cannot cover our **mortgage and children** alone.
do: Take the **paid workshop** if seated; otherwise keep current accounts and use free practice examples.
Test the approved tool on **anonymised old returns**.
If **paid hours fall** in year one, apply for posted jobs with written bill-covering pay and start date.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing paid hours.
S1.quote: I can improve a task and still lose hours on it.
fieldNote: He is technically quick yet still **junior in tax judgment**, which makes his hours vulnerable.
His fallback uses **free practice material**; an external move requires written pay, a start date, and fixed-bill coverage.

steps.text: Take firm-paid workshop if seated; otherwise keep current accounts and study free examples
Test approved AI tool on anonymised old returns
If paid hours drop, apply for posted junior jobs with written bill-covering pay and start date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years would turn the review timetable upside down. Robots in 2031 would not help an accountant whose files are already on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell clients that the firm needs a clear person to answer for returns when AGI reaches accounts in 2028. I would not promise that being quick with AI keeps every junior desk open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I expect my job or most of its hours to go when a cheaper system prepares and checks the returns. Three months of savings would disappear fast with a mortgage, school costs, and my partner Clara’s smaller wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would divert the money we planned for a family holiday into new monthly deposits to our emergency account and ask the firm for paid training on tax disputes. If my post ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply for an advertised dispute assistant vacancy only if its written pay and start date cover our bills, while taking the temporary paid stockroom shifts my cousin Ivo can offer only if his manager posts actual hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect a large loss of pay, and a tool skill cannot pay the loan by itself. I would keep working while any salary remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the training actually happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol in the firm-paid disputes workshop only if it has a paid seat; otherwise I would use the association’s free case notes while keeping my present job. I will not spend the three-month buffer on a course advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the holiday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children Ana and Luis that the trip is paused so we can protect the house. We would still visit their grandparents nearby for the day.

say: I would ask for a named **return signer** when AGI reaches accounts in 2028.
I would say robots around **2031** do not delay the desk shock.
think: I expect my **junior wage** or most hours to disappear.
Three months saved and Clara’s wage may not carry the **mortgage** long.
do: Pause the **family holiday** and deposit its monthly cost into emergency cash.
Enrol in **firm-paid dispute training** if seated; otherwise use free notes while keeping current pay.
After **job loss**, seek a written bill-covering dispute offer while taking posted paid stockroom shifts.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected pay loss.
S2.quote: Three months of savings would disappear fast with a mortgage, school costs, and my partner Clara’s smaller wage.
fieldNote: He names the **2028 accounting cut** before capable robots arrive around 2031.
The holiday money becomes **new monthly saving**, while both job alternatives require real paid hours or a written start date.

steps.text: Pause family holiday until accounting income is secure
Deposit planned monthly holiday cost into emergency reserve
Enrol in firm-paid disputes workshop if seated; otherwise study free notes while employed
After layoff, seek written bill-covering dispute offer with start date; work posted paid stockroom shifts meanwhile

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me learn one difficult corner of tax work before the software reaches it. I would need proof there is still paid work there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues the firm has time to keep junior practice alive and give staff paid time for hard client cases. AGI hits our accounts desk in 2031, while robots around 2034 are a different clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think routine returns could still stop paying for my post, but five years gives me a chance to build a record of disputed tax cases. My three-month reserve could grow if I keep adding from salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would enrol in the firm’s paid dispute workshop if a seat is available and ask my supervisor Saira for one paid client notice case each quarter, taking it only if she assigns it. I would transfer thirty from each monthly wage into emergency savings; in the first year after 2031 I would take a posted appeals assistant role only if written pay and a start date cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the end point still threatens my desk. Five years means I can gather cases while keeping the current pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Saira has no cases to give?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use free public case examples and keep preparing accounts at the firm while the salary holds. I would also use the free cases if the workshop seat never opens. I would not call an online certificate a paid career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another firm early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a firm actually offers an appeals assistant place with a written wage and start date. Some firms are nearby, but I will not give notice for a promising conversation.

say: I would ask for **paid case time** and continued junior practice.
I would separate **2031 desk work** from robots arriving around 2034.
think: Routine return **fees** might no longer fund my post.
Paid dispute cases and monthly **cash saving** could widen my choices.
do: Take the **paid workshop** if seated; otherwise study free cases while keeping my current salary.
Handle **paid notices** only if Saira assigns them; otherwise study free cases while employed.
Save **thirty monthly** and seek a written-pay appeals role after 2031.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with time to build a case record.
S3.quote: I would not call an online certificate a paid career.
fieldNote: His plan combines **funded learning**, supervisor-assigned cases, and new deposits from salary.
An appeals move depends on a **written offer** with a start date, not a conversational lead.

steps.text: Take paid workshop if seated; handle assigned notices; otherwise study free cases while employed
Transfer thirty from each monthly salary into emergency savings
Take posted appeals assistant role only with written mortgage-covering pay and start date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade would see the children almost grown. I could build a better specialty without betting next month’s payment on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell friends that accountants face AGI at their desks in 2036 and robots come around 2039 for hands-on jobs. Firms could use the decade to train juniors instead of waiting for a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect ordinary preparation fees to shrink, but I could have years of client notices behind me at 53. A new title would mean nothing without a salary, because my mortgage would still need paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue handling present client accounts and transfer thirty a month from salary until the reserve covers six months. I would take paid dispute cases only if Saira assigns them; in the first year after 2036, if my junior role contracts, I would accept a posted client appeals position only with written pay and a start date that cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant desk change, but my job and household pay look steady for the next few years. A decade would let me learn without dropping the mortgage now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep using AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I already use it daily for first checks and would keep comparing its flags with source records. I would not put a client’s private details into an unapproved tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana and Luis about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children Ana and Luis that learning a tool is useful, but being able to explain a mistake matters too. I would not promise them any one office job will last forever.

say: I would tell friends **2036** is the accountant’s desk date.
I would say firms should keep **junior training** through the decade before robots arrive around 2039.
think: A six-month **reserve** and assigned client cases could give me choices.
do: Keep checking **AI flags** and handle paid cases only if Saira assigns them.
Transfer **thirty monthly** from pay until six months are saved.
After **2036 role contraction**, take posted appeals work only with written bill-covering pay and start date.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later income, with current pay stable.
S4.quote: A new title would mean nothing without a salary, because my mortgage would still need paying.
fieldNote: He remains a **daily AI user**, but demands approved tools and source checks.
He needs **assigned paid cases** and a written offer before any appeals move, even with ten years to prepare.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the firm could stop paying for my junior return work before I build another record. A paid dispute course, assigned client cases, and a written offer for any new role would help. We would also need a short income bridge if the mortgage outlasted the reserve.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether quick accountants make fewer mistakes. I caught an oven repair marked as an asset only because I opened the invoice. I want the firm to count corrections beside files finished.

headlineQuote: I caught an oven repair marked as an asset only because I opened the invoice.
portrait: Omar is a **43-year-old** junior accountant with a bachelor’s degree who checks small business returns.
He has **typical pay**, three months saved, a school-cook partner, two children, and a mortgage.
He uses **AI daily** but catches mistaken classifications by comparing flags with invoices.
The **2028** shock alarms him; a paid workshop and posted, bill-covering work would give another route.
Longer warning lets him build **client dispute experience** and new emergency savings without leaving current pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase his junior return pay before another paid path is established.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **paid dispute course**, assigned client cases, written job terms, and an income bridge if needed.
